entries.markdown: [#975](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/pull/975) [`906780b`](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/commit/906780b9e8c05d44e282f54053e892dbf428cfaf) Thanks [@l7aromeo](https://github.com/l7aromeo)! - `@MeoCord({ answerDenied: true })` answers a guard's `false` on an interaction as if the guard had thrown `GuardDeniedError`. A command, context menu, component or modal a guard denies is told privately "You can't use this." in the user's language, from `meocord.guard.denied`, which an app's catalogs translate; until now a denied command got Discord's "The application did not respond". The denial takes a thrown one's path: a filter catching `GuardDeniedError` sees it and can answer otherwise, observers get the outcome `'denied'` with `deniedBy` and the error, and a call with `@Defer` is answered into its deferral. Autocomplete still closes its menu, an event handler still skips the event, and a message command stays silent, since a `false` there is often a filter. A guard that throws its own `GuardDeniedError` keeps its words. In a testing module built from an app that sets the option, `invoke` rejects with that `GuardDeniedError` for a guard's `false` and sends nothing, as it does for a thrown denial, while `dispatch` answers it as the bot does. Nothing changes until an app sets the option. See [https://meocord.dev/docs/4.3/guards](/docs/4.3/guards).

[#980](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/pull/980) [`0510d95`](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/commit/0510d957c5f807cb720c6542881e9c2cc94fa8a5) Thanks [@l7aromeo](https://github.com/l7aromeo)! - `bindTheme` now runs each call in the theme of the member and server it answers. A function it wraps rebuilds the theme for every call whose arguments name a server or a user, as a handler's call is themed (an interaction, a message, a reaction, a member): MeoCord's defaults and the app's theme, the `@UseTheme` layers of the handler that bound it, then `themeFor`'s layers for that call's server and user, in the order a handler's call has them. A collector's `collect` callback answers each member who clicks in their own theme, and a `client.on(...)` listener bound in one server's call answers every other server in that server's theme, where both used the theme of the member whose call bound them.

A theme `themeFor` is still looking up replaces the handler's once found, so the wrapped function stays synchronous: `respond()` waits for it, and `useTheme()` reads the handler's theme until then. A call whose arguments name neither, such as a collector's `end`, runs in the whole theme of the call that bound it, as before. Once a bot's stop or a testing module's `close()` has ended its shutdown, a wrapped function asks no `themeFor` resolver: a call whose arguments name a server or a user runs in the theme of the handler that bound it, and nothing is logged for the lookup. An app without `themeFor` sees no change. See [Theming](/docs/4.3/theming#collectors-and-listeners).

[#979](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/pull/979) [`1789503`](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/commit/1789503db4590eef28769fe9eae07171ed9bcb3d) Thanks [@l7aromeo](https://github.com/l7aromeo)! - Under Bun, what the runtime prints itself names your source, as under Node: `console.error(error)` and any other inspection of an error, an uncaught error, and a rejection nothing handles. `sourceMappedStacks` mapped only `error.stack`, so a crash, the trace most worth reading, showed positions in `dist/main.js`.

When the bundle maps its stacks (`sourceMappedStacks` is not `false` and the build wrote its source map), a bot running on Bun gets:

- an inspection hook on `Error.prototype` (`Symbol.for('nodejs.util.inspect.custom')`), which inspects an error with its mapped stack and keeps its own properties, such as a `DiscordAPIError`'s `code`, and its `cause`;
- an `uncaughtException` and an `unhandledRejection` listener on `process`, which print the error with its mapped stack and end the process as Bun would: code 1 for an uncaught error, and for a rejection as Bun's `--unhandled-rejections` mode decides. Without the flag a rejection ends the process; under `=throw` it is raised as an uncaught error, which your own `uncaughtException` listener gets, or which ends the process when there is none.

What Bun prints changes with it. `console.error(error)` and a crash print the error in Node's inspection format, `Error: message` followed by `at` lines naming `src/` files and any own properties in braces, where Bun printed its own layout: the source line excerpt above the error and, for a crash, the `Bun v…` line below it are gone. An error whose `stack` is no string of its own, such as a `DOMException` or one with a `stack` getter, is printed by Bun's own formatter, so a crash still shows its name and message. Under `--unhandled-rejections=warn`, Bun prints its own warning for a rejection, which keeps the bundle's positions. Set `sourceMappedStacks: false` to keep Bun's own output.

`process.listenerCount()` for each of the two events is one higher. An application that listens for either event itself, before or after MeoCord, keeps the error and the exit, also with a listener that removes itself as it runs, as `process.once` adds one: MeoCord's listener does nothing while another listener is there. The exception is a listener that runs ahead of MeoCord's and removes itself, as one added after MeoCord's with `process.prependOnceListener` does: it is gone by the time MeoCord's listener runs, so MeoCord also reports the error and exits 1. Under Node nothing changes. See [Configuration](/docs/4.3/configuration).

[#993](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/pull/993) [`264b19d`](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/commit/264b19db0a119f318eec78763148d01e7034fff8) Thanks [@l7aromeo](https://github.com/l7aromeo)! - MeoCord's CommonJS build bundles its ES-module-only dependencies, `inversify` (with its `@inversifyjs/*` packages) and `chalk`, so `require('meocord/...')` loads nothing that ships only as an ES module. jest, which runs tests as CommonJS, now loads `meocord/testing` without Node's VM modules: drop `NODE_OPTIONS=--experimental-vm-modules` from a jest setup that added it for MeoCord. With the flag left in, jest runs as before. The ES module build imports both packages from `node_modules` as before. A process that loads both builds runs two copies of `inversify` and of `chalk`: the one bundled into the CommonJS build and the one in `node_modules` that the ES module build imports. The two builds' `Logger` writes the same output under each colour setting. With them, and with the rest of 4.3, `dist/cjs` is 1765 KB, where 4.2.3's was 1227 KB, and THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md carries the bundled packages' licenses. See [https://meocord.dev/docs/4.3/testing](/docs/4.3/testing).

[#976](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/pull/976) [`77d534b`](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/commit/77d534bfc76eedb5f1e9c900649ff715e9bb03e9) Thanks [@l7aromeo](https://github.com/l7aromeo)! - New `commandMention(path, target)` in `meocord/common` gives a clickable mention of one of your slash commands, a subcommand or a grouped subcommand, such as `</settings channel:1234567890123456789>`, so a help reply or an error can point at the command to run:

```ts
await respond(interaction).send(`Set a channel first with ${await commandMention('settings channel', interaction)}.`)
```

`target` is the interaction, message, guild or client the mention is shown with. It looks the command up where the reader can use it: the target's guild first, then the global commands. The IDs come from the bot's own registration, or from one request per scope on its first mention, listed again when no scope holds it, so it works in a shard, with `commands.register: false`, and for commands `meocord register` sent. A path the app doesn't declare is a `RangeError`; a command that isn't registered where the reader is, or a mention before the bot is ready, is an `Error` that says what to do. A scope whose listing fails, such as a guild the bot lost access to, doesn't stop a mention the global scope resolves; if none does, the `Error` names the failure.

In tests, a testing module answers from the commands its controllers declare, with a fixed ID per command and no request; `MeoCordTestingModule.create({ … }).overrideCommandId(name, id)` sets one. See [Formatting](/docs/4.3/formatting).

[#978](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/pull/978) [`4d52db9`](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/commit/4d52db9d611b7759ac1184d1d85b674a3536f5e4) Thanks [@l7aromeo](https://github.com/l7aromeo)! - `meocord/common` exports `formatDuration(ms, target?, options?)`, which writes a length of time for people: `formatDuration(3_900_000)` is `1h 5m`, and `{ style: 'long' }` gives `1 hour, 5 minutes`. Given an interaction or a message, it writes in that user's or server's language through your app's translator; given a `Locale`, through `options.t`. `units`, `largest`, `smallest` and `round` choose what it shows, and `{ style: 'param' }` writes `1h30m`, which a `{x:duration}` param reads back, for a value up to `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` milliseconds. See [Formatting](/docs/4.3/formatting).

Its unit words are new MeoCord texts in a `meocord.duration` group, the first of MeoCord's texts with plural forms, which an app's catalog translates like the others, with every plural form its language needs. `defineCatalog` refuses at compile time a translation of one of them without its `other` form, with a form that isn't a text, or with a key that is no plural category. `expectCompleteCatalog` now reports a translation of MeoCord's own plural texts that lacks a form its language needs, such as `few` in Russian, or that isn't a plural, `{}` included. See [Localisation](/docs/4.3/localisation).

A plural in a catalog with a form that isn't a text, as a JSON catalog may hold, reads as missing, so the next locale's catalog answers; translating it threw a `TypeError`.

`cooldownMessage` writes its wait with `formatDuration`, and its output is unchanged for every finite wait. A refusal whose wait is no finite number, as a custom `CooldownStore` may answer, now tells the caller "Slow down: try again later.", a new MeoCord text `meocord.cooldown.later` that an app's catalog translates, where they were shown a timestamp Discord couldn't display; `cooldownMessage` gives the same text where it wrote `NaNd NaNh`.

[#978](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/pull/978) [`43396b2`](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/commit/43396b2efe4508e1de46972a28235197cbd19bcc) Thanks [@l7aromeo](https://github.com/l7aromeo)! - `meocord/common` exports `permissionNames(permissions, target?, options?)`, which names permissions as a server owner reads them in Discord's role settings: `permissionNames(['ManageMessages', 'BanMembers'])` is `['Ban Members', 'Manage Messages']`, in bit order, and `{ join: 'and' }` gives `Ban Members and Manage Messages`, joined as a list in the labels' language. The labels are Discord's own wording, commas included, such as `Kick, Approve, and Reject Members`. Given an interaction or a message, it names them in that user's or server's language through your app's translator; given a `Locale`, through `options.t`. A bit with two flag names, such as `1 << 30`, gives one label; a bit with no label gives its flag name, and a bit discord.js doesn't name gives `Unknown permission (1 << n)`. See [Formatting](/docs/4.3/formatting).

The labels are new MeoCord texts in a `meocord.permissions` group, by flag name, which an app's catalog translates like the others. See [Localisation](/docs/4.3/localisation).

[#978](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/pull/978) [`768018f`](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/commit/768018f8f95498273a15893f90fe1208fa409a9b) Thanks [@l7aromeo](https://github.com/l7aromeo)! - `meocord/common` exports discord.js's formatters under their own names, so a bot imports its formatting from one place: `userMention`, `channelMention`, `time` with `TimestampStyles`, `bold`, `codeBlock`, `escapeMarkdown` and the rest, 44 functions and constants and 4 types. They are your own discord.js's functions, not copies: `userMention` from `meocord/common` is `userMention` from `discord.js`, so code that imports them from discord.js keeps working, and their documentation is discord.js's. `version` and the deprecated `underscore` aren't exported. A new app's sample button replies with `userMention(ownerId)`. See [Formatting](/docs/4.3/formatting).

[#978](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/pull/978) [`7683c01`](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/commit/7683c014a613a5374bb8dc8d041b4117eefdbcf7) Thanks [@l7aromeo](https://github.com/l7aromeo)! - `meocord/common` exports `splitMessage`, `truncate` and `DiscordLimits` for fitting text to what Discord accepts. `splitMessage(text)` splits text into messages of at most 2000 characters, or the `max` you give it: at line ends, a longer line at its last whitespace, never through an emoji or an accented letter. It reads code as Discord does, and closes code cut across messages at the end of one and reopens it in the next, a code block with its language and inline code with its own backticks, so each message shows its part of the text as the whole text does. `truncate(text, max)` shortens text to `max` characters with an ellipsis, closing code it cuts open. `DiscordLimits` names Discord's length limits, such as `DiscordLimits.content` and `DiscordLimits.embedDescription`. See [Formatting](/docs/4.3/formatting).

The help reply, MeoCord's own and a `presenter.messageHelp` string, splits with `splitMessage`. It splits as before, with these differences: a code block or inline code cut across messages is closed and reopened rather than cut through, no cut parts an escape from the character it escapes or leaves a backtick to pair with another in its message, a line longer than a message breaks at its last whitespace rather than at its last character, dropping the whitespace there, and a CR before a line end is no longer left at the end of a message. See the [upgrade guide](/docs/4.3/migrating#help-reply-split).

[#1006](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/pull/1006) [`7a633ff`](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/commit/7a633ff0edddb79263cdd97dda34fa6035d2f491) Thanks [@l7aromeo](https://github.com/l7aromeo)! - Two changes the next major version (5.0) makes at compile time are now announced:

- A context menu handler that declares a second parameter is named in a startup warning, and by a testing module as it compiles. A context menu command has no options, so that argument is always `{}`; remove it. In 5.0 such a handler fails to compile. The check reads the method's parameter count, so a second parameter with a default value, or a rest parameter, goes unnamed. See [Context menus](/docs/4.3/context-menus).
- `@Autocomplete<T>(…)`'s type argument is deprecated, and your editor strikes it through. It did nothing: the handler's return type is inferred. Write `@Autocomplete(…)`; in 5.0 the type argument fails to compile. See [Autocomplete](/docs/4.3/autocomplete).

[#977](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/pull/977) [`d8e80b3`](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/commit/d8e80b3902890d96d7d99bcafb907a1953ddc7c5) Thanks [@l7aromeo](https://github.com/l7aromeo)! - A testing module can answer an event handler's refusals as the bot does. With `eventFallback: true` in `MeoCordTestingModule.create()` or `fromApp()`, `emit` runs the bot's own event fallback: a guard's `GuardDeniedError` skips the event and the handler isn't counted as run, and a `UserError` is answered as a reply to the newest message among the event's arguments, with the app's presenter and `replyEmoji`. Neither rejects `emit`; any other error still does. The option applies to `emit` alone, not to `invoke` of an `@On` handler. With the option, `emit` gives each event argument's client the module's presenter, theme and translator without strict mocks too, so the reply is drawn as the bot draws it. A test can now check the reply a member gets:

```ts
const module = MeoCordTestingModule.fromApp(App, { eventFallback: true }).compile()
const message = createMockMessage({ content: 'hello' })
await module.emit('messageCreate', message)
expect(message.reply).toHaveBeenCalled()
```

Without the option `emit` rejects with both errors as before, and the first time it does, it logs one warning for the run: the next major version (5.0) answers them as the bot does ([#964](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/issues/964)). Set `eventFallback: false` to keep the rejection without the warning. See [Invoke and dispatch](/docs/4.3/invoke-and-dispatch).

[#984](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/pull/984) [`85314bc`](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/commit/85314bc292b20e364beb283fb415688e8c229f6b) Thanks [@l7aromeo](https://github.com/l7aromeo)! - `meocord generate controller` and `meocord generate observer` now add the class they write to `src/app.ts`: its import after your last import, and its entry in `@MeoCord({ controllers })` or `@MeoCord({ observers })`, adding `observers` when the options have none. A controller or observer takes no part until it is listed, and the step was easy to miss. The edit is made with your project's own `typescript` and inserts only those lines, following the list's layout, indentation and trailing comma; nothing else in the file changes. When your project has ESLint, found from its root as Node finds packages, including one a workspace keeps in a parent folder, the edited file is linted with it, with no fixing, as your app's lint runs it; an edit that would bring an error the file didn't have, such as an import a rule forbids or a line past Prettier's print width, is undone, and the file is left as it was, its modification time included. The file is written in place, as an editor saves it: its mode, owner and links stay, a symlinked `src/app.ts` edits its target, and one you can't write is refused. Because a typed ESLint config lints the file on disk, the edit is there while it is checked, so `start --dev` rebuilds twice for an edit that is undone, and three times for one kept in a file that already had lint errors. Ctrl+C, or a SIGTERM outside Windows, while the edit is being checked puts the file back first. When ESLint is missing, can't run or doesn't finish, the class is listed and `generate` says it went unchecked and why. Pass `--skip-app` to keep the old behaviour, which leaves `src/app.ts` alone and prints what to add.

When the class can't be placed safely, `generate` writes its files, warns why, prints the two lines to add and changes nothing in `src/app.ts`: when the file or its `@MeoCord({ … })` is missing; the list is not an array written in place (a variable, an import or a call) or holds a spread; the options have a spread or a computed key that may already hold the list; the class's name is already taken in `src/app.ts`, by a type-only import, an import from another file or a declaration of its own; the edit would fail your lint; or the project's `typescript` can't be loaded or has no compiler API on its main entry, as with TypeScript 7. A class already imported and listed is left alone. Other kinds, such as services and guards, are used by naming them in code and keep printing their hint. ESLint gets 60 seconds across the runs `generate` makes, including the one that formats the files it writes: a run still going then is stopped, and killed if it ignores the request, no further run starts, and a warning says the files went unformatted or the edit unchecked, so a config that never finishes no longer holds `generate` for good. Its report is read from a file of its own, so a config that prints does not leave the edit unchecked. See [CLI](/docs/4.3/cli).

[#975](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/pull/975) [`0630ee4`](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/commit/0630ee4f675a345825534fd26aa3469aa28dd12c) Thanks [@l7aromeo](https://github.com/l7aromeo)! - `@MeoCord({ globalStagesOnEvents: false })` keeps the app's global guards and interceptors that declare no `types` from running before `@On` and `@Once` handlers. They still run for commands, components, modals, message commands, reactions and autocomplete, so a global blocklist or maintenance guard keeps covering message commands. A stage that declares `types` keeps exactly what it declares, `'event'` included; the guards and interceptors a controller or a handler names, and global exception filters, are unaffected. The default stays `true` in 4.3 and becomes `false` in the next major version (5.0), as [meocord#502](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/issues/502) plans.

The startup line that named each such stage is now a warning, once per stage, shown only when the app has event handlers and leaves the option unset. To silence it, declare `@Guard({ types: [...] })` or `@Interceptor({ types: [...] })` on the stage, or set `globalStagesOnEvents` to `true` to keep today's behaviour or to `false` to take 5.0's now. See [https://meocord.dev/docs/4.3/guards](/docs/4.3/guards).

[#1004](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/pull/1004) [`8c63674`](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/commit/8c636741b4b6157e6fc9b6c2fc875751f0bd389f) Thanks [@l7aromeo](https://github.com/l7aromeo)! - The built-in help reads what joins its lists from two new MeoCord texts: `meocord.help.listJoiner`, a comma and a space, joins a command's aliases, and `meocord.help.paramJoiner`, a middle dot with a space on each side, its params. A catalog that translates `meocord.help` can write them as its language writes a list, such as `、` in Chinese or Japanese. A catalog without them shows the help as before. `expectCompleteCatalog(t, { meocord: true })` lists both as missing in a locale that doesn't translate them. See [Localisation](/docs/4.3/localisation).

[#977](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/pull/977) [`5dd3eaf`](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/commit/5dd3eaffad1c5e4a63708a8680515218e3415156) Thanks [@l7aromeo](https://github.com/l7aromeo)! - `inspectHandler()` reports a handler's `@Defer` as `defer`: the options it runs with, with their defaults filled in (`ephemeral: false`, `suppressNotifications: false`, `disable: 'all'`, `mode: 'eager'`, and `after: 1500` for `mode: 'auto'`), or `undefined` without one. A `@Defer` inherited from the method a handler overrides is reported as the bot applies it. A test can check that a command defers privately without dispatching it:

```ts
expect(inspectHandler(PingController, 'ping').defer).toEqual({
  ephemeral: true,
  suppressNotifications: false,
  disable: 'all',
  mode: 'eager',
})
```

`toEqual` on a whole inspection doesn't compare `defer`, so existing assertions hold. See [Invoke and dispatch](/docs/4.3/invoke-and-dispatch).

[#1004](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/pull/1004) [`7046f51`](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/commit/7046f516e7e13710f104e222f6362d4c51b1824e) Thanks [@l7aromeo](https://github.com/l7aromeo)! - `t.localizations(key, params)` takes a message with `{params}` and fills them into each locale's translation, where that translation places them, so descriptions that differ by one word need one catalog key, not one per word. The params are typed from the default message, as `t()`'s are. A value is a word or a number, used in every locale, or a function of the locale for a value that is itself translated: `t.localizations('lookup.user', { mode: locale => t.locale(locale)('modes.chaos') })`. The function is called once for each locale whose message uses it. A value, static or from a function, is used as written: a `{param}` in it stays as text, as `t()` leaves it. A translator typed `Translator<any>`, or by hand with messages typed `string` (a JSON file's shape), takes any params for such a message. A param the default message takes and `params` leave out, or give as `undefined`, throws, naming each one. `t.localizations(key)` without params is unchanged; for a message that takes params, its error now names the params to give. `ParamLocalizationKey`, `LocalizationParam` and `LocalizationParams` are exported from `meocord/common`, to type a helper that takes such a key or builds its params before passing them on. On a `Translator` without its catalog type, `t.localizations(key, params)` and `ParamLocalizationKey` give the same "This Translator has no catalog type" error as its other methods. See [Localisation](/docs/4.3/localisation).

[#1014](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/pull/1014) [`c86a086`](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/commit/c86a08677d395bb3fb15f39a63f8ab42792175e6) Thanks [@l7aromeo](https://github.com/l7aromeo)! - Under `useStrictMocks()`, a mock answers a property its discord.js class does not have as discord.js does: it reads `undefined` and is not `in` the mock, so `message.isRepliable?.()` gives `undefined` and `if (value.guild)` is false for a class without a `guild`, as on a bot. `in` is true for a field the class sets on its instances, such as `'content' in message`; the fields are read from the source of the discord.js the application installed. A property a test gives or assigns, one the class has, and a mock of an app's own subclass answer as before. Without `useStrictMocks()` a mock keeps its placeholder, and the first read of such a property by an app's or a test's code logs one warning for the run, naming the property, its class and what strict mocks answer; MeoCord's own reads and the discord.js code a mock runs stay quiet. The next major version (5.0) answers `undefined` without the call. See [Mocks](/docs/4.3/mocks).

[#977](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/pull/977) [`de3e228`](https://github.com/meocord/meocord/commit/de3e22897ba723a01f465d7c0cba0ef649a1f21d) Thanks [@l7aromeo](https://github.com/l7aromeo)! - Under `useStrictMocks()`, `createMockClient()` has a working emitter, so a test can attach a collector-style listener to the mock client and see what depends on it:

- `on()`, `once()`, `off()`, `emit()`, `listeners()`, `listenerCount()` and the emitter's other methods stay mock functions that record each call, and call through to discord.js's, so `client.on.mock.calls` and `toHaveBeenCalledWith` work as before and a test can still set its own behaviour. `client.on(...)` returns the client instead of `undefined`, `listeners()` and `listenerCount()` answer, and `emit()` reaches every listener attached. discord.js's own `InteractionCollector` made on the client works, filtered by a message, in a server or a direct message, by a response, as `createMessageComponentCollector()` builds one, by a channel, a server or a component type, and it ends when its message, channel or server is deleted. For that, a message an interaction sends names it in `interactionMetadata`, as Discord's do, and a command's `message` and a message's raw `channel_id` and `guild_id` read `undefined`, as on discord.js's classes, where they read a placeholder. A strict test that read one of those, or a member of the placeholder, now gets `undefined`: a command's `interaction.message.id` throws a `TypeError`, and `message.guild_id` is `undefined`. An interaction's `authorizingIntegrationOwners` is discord.js's `AuthorizingIntegrationOwners` for an app installed to a server, keyed to the interaction's server or `"0"` in a direct message with the bot, as Discord sends it, where it was the mock's placeholder object; the message's `interactionMetadata` holds the same owners. With `themeFor`, a call in a direct message looks no server up, so a test that expected the guild resolver to be asked for a mock message's generated server there sees no call.
- `module.dispatch()` leaves a component or modal no route takes to the mock client's `interactionCreate` listeners, as the bot leaves it to a collector: it delivers the interaction to them, in the order they were attached, and answers "no handler matched" only if none answered. - A call waits for the hooks of its handler's class, the guards, interceptors, filters and pipes that run for it, global ones included, the presenter, the `themeFor` class, and what each of them injects. It doesn't wait for a hook ordered after all of those. The hooks still run one at a time, so it also waits for a slower hook ordered before its own.

A lookup follows what Discord has been told of its interaction, as the call does: once Discord has an acknowledgement or an answer, it waits as long as the hooks run; while one is on its way, it waits for the outcome, neither going ahead nor warning; told nothing, as without `@Defer`, it waits until 2 seconds after the interaction was created, or 2 seconds from the first wait for it for one with no creation time or one ahead of the clock, which its warning then reads as "after waiting 2.0 s", then goes ahead with a warning, at once if those have passed. A call and the lookups for its interaction waiting at once go ahead together, on one decision: the call first, its warning naming the hook, and the lookups then without one of their own; a lookup that starts once that decision is made follows the rule afresh. An autocomplete's waits 1 second the same way. `@Defer({ mode: 'auto' })`'s acknowledgement counts as on its way from the call's start until it is sent or an answer's Discord call replaces it; an answer still waiting for its theme doesn't hold it back, and goes out after it, as an edit, the acknowledgement as private as that answer, whatever `@Defer`'s `ephemeral` says. The warning: `PrefsThemes looked up a theme before onReady in Prefs had settled, 2.0 s after the interaction was created, as long as an interaction Discord has been told nothing of waits. Make onReady in Prefs faster.`

- An interaction without `@Defer` waits until 2 seconds after it was created and an autocomplete 1 second, then runs, with one warning per hook naming it, whatever `warnSlow` says: `PricesController.price ran before onReady in PriceCache had settled, 2.0 s after the interaction was created, as long as an interaction without @Defer waits. Add @Defer to PricesController.price to have it wait for the hook, or make onReady in PriceCache faster.` A message, a reaction and an event wait as long as the hooks run.
- That wait and the wait for `themeFor` share one deadline, 2 seconds after the interaction was created (1 second for an autocomplete), leaving the handler the last second for its answer. With a hook that runs past it, a resolver the hook holds back misses the call even when it answers quickly: the answer goes out at 2 seconds in the handler's theme, and the next call reads the theme from the cache. A call whose hook was late logs the hook's warning alone, not the theme lookup's.
- Under `@Defer({ mode: 'auto' })`, with `waitForReady` on or off, an answer still waiting for its theme, such as from a slow `themeFor` resolver, no longer cancels the acknowledgement: the interaction is acknowledged on time, as privately as that answer, and the answer then edits it in. - A hook that throws counts as settled.
- A stop (`app.stop()`, a signal's shutdown, or `MeoCordTestingModule.close()`) decides every call still waiting where it stops waiting for the calls under way, before the `onShutdown` hooks: by the end of the event loop iteration's timers and I/O, before its immediates.
